answers.text: So the rule: always three lines, in order — delivery date, item and quantity, and change from the order, or 'no change'. If the email is missing one, put 'not confirmed' on that line instead of guessing. It stays consistent because that's what I told it to do.

Tell it: one line per claim — date, amount, category, person — same order, then a total at the bottom that's the sum of the amount column. If two lines share the same date, amount and person, count them once and note 'duplicate, counted once' rather than adding both.

The price checks out, 100 times €48.50 is €4,850. The real issue is the dates: call on the 14th, delivery revised to the 19th, but it also calls the 19th 'three days out from today' — that only fits if today was the 16th, which sits oddly next to a call on the 14th. I'd double check that before it goes out.

62 up from 54 is right, about 15% more. But 3 late out of 62 is closer to 95%, not the 97% written. The 340 units across the depots add up fine, but it's odd stock 'held steady' the same week deliveries rose 15% — worth asking why. I'd go back over both before it goes up the chain.

I'd sign off the second one, it shows €25,100 and €612,000 and the sum. The first just gives 4.1% with nothing behind it — if that's wrong there's no way to spot it from the sentence alone. Could well be right, just impossible to tell from what's written.

I'd send the second one, the order and credit references are right there, so anyone can find exactly what was applied. The first says 'this was entirely our error' without saying how anyone would know that — can't really be checked as it stands. Not that the first is wrong, it would just need a look-over first.

1. No — customer's personal detail, wouldn't paste that into an uncleared tool. 2. Yes — just a total figure, no names attached. 3. No — not released yet, a real problem if it got out. 4. Yes — already public on our website. 5. No — someone's personal number, not mine to hand over.

Pricing and volume discounts I wouldn't paste in as they are, that's the sensitive part. Same with the confidentiality clause, since it names both companies. The delivery schedule is fine as is, nothing sensitive in dates on their own. Registration details I'd leave out too, just to be safe.

Before it goes to the manager, I'd cross-check the delivery total and on-time percentage against the warehouse system directly, not just re-read the sentence. I'd do that every week, right after the draft is written and before it's sent up, checking two or three figures against source. That would catch a wrong total, not just a spelling mistake.

Step 4 needs the gate — once the confirmation goes out automatically, it's hard to take back if step 1 or 2 went wrong earlier. Step 1 matters too, since a wrong item there carries through everything, but step 4 is where the mistake reaches the customer. The gate should hold if the stock check is right on the edge, or the quantity looks unusually high.
